title: A Strong Mandate Amid Falling Participation
content:
On 3 October, Latvians elected a new parliament. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ regionalist, green and conservative United List (Latvian: Apvienotais saraksts, AS) more than doubled its seats, from 15 to 41. The answer to the question, however, whether the country ‘woke up to a new reality’ after these elections is both no and yes.

No, because our government will apparently be almost the same as it was before the election. Yes, because, for the first time in many years, one party has secured such a substantial lead that it can form a coalition with virtually any other political force elected to the 15th Saeima, the Latvian parliament, except the liberal-conservative ‘New Unity’ alliance. A three-party coalition would now be needed for building a broad and balanced coalition government.

title: The vote is harder to steal, but politics remains hard to change
content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s general elections on 4 October produced an unusual result: the country has taken a significant step forward in how votes are cast and counted, without fundamentally changing who holds political power. The familiar names remain at the centre. The Serb nationalist Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), led by the pro-Russian separatist leader Milorad Dodik, retains its dominant position in the Republika Srpska, the Bosnian entity, ; the Croat nationalist party Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) is set to regain the Croat seat in the three-member Presidency; and the Social Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina (SDP BiH) has retained the Bosniak seat through Denis Bećirović.

Meanwhile, politics in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has become more fragmented, with the centre-right Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina (SBiH) making a strong comeback.

title: The missing engine of Europe’s renewal
content:
From climate collapse and industrial stagnation to popular discontent and the rise of authoritarianism, our democratic future and social fabric are under unprecedented strain. The report commissioned by the Spanish government, Two Promises to Those Who Work: Voice and Ownership, delivers a clear diagnosis: our societies face nine interrelated crises, from ecological overshoot and the disruptive rise of AI to the erosion of trust in institutions and predatory financialisation.

The insight that can give hope is that the various crises share a single common denominator: an extractivist corporate model that treats workers as disposable resources rather than citizens. Extending the democratic project into the economy by recognising workers’ access to voice and ownership – the two pillars of economic democracy – is the only structural antidote to a trend that will otherwise destroy political democracy.

title: Living better while living longer
content:
Europeans are living longer. This is one of the achievements of our social model. The question is whether we are living those additional years in good physical and mental health and whether this progress is shared equally across society.

The pursuit of longevity cannot simply mean adding years to life. It just as well means adding life to those years. In other words, extending the time in which we can take a full part in society, keep our relationships, feel accomplished and live with dignity. Importantly, though, healthy longevity must not become another privilege that correlates with income or social status. The right to healthy longevity needs to become an imperative of the progressive agenda for Europe.

What kind of prevention?

title: Equal rights, unequal choices: making gender equality real for Gen Z
content:
What does gender equality mean if you can work full-time and still not afford to live independently, or if caring for others comes at the cost of your career? For Gen Z, equality cannot be reduced to rights on paper. It must mean having the real freedom and the material means to choose how to live.

Gen Z has grown up with more formal gender equality than any previous generation. Yet the material freedom needed to make that equality real is becoming harder to secure. Young people have more rights, more awareness and more freedom on paper, but increasingly fewer of the material conditions needed to turn that freedom into real choices.

So, what does it mean to be equal? If you cannot afford to leave your parents’ home, if you are forced to leave your region to get a job, if caring for others means giving up your career, or if having children is economically unfeasible, equality on paper starts to look very different in practice. For Gen Z and the generations to come, gender equality must mean more than equal rights: it must mean an equal capacity to exercise those rights and build an independent life.

title: Gen Z’s political divide isn’t really about gender
content:
Progressives risk misreading Generation Z by treating social media, the manosphere and changing gender norms as the main explanation for young people’s political divergence. These forces matter. But the evidence points to something deeper: economic insecurity, institutional distrust and individualisation are shaping an entire generation, even if men and women often express that malaise differently.

When progressives discuss young people, one story increasingly dominates. Young men are drifting to the right because TikTok, YouTube and the manosphere expose them to antifeminist ideas; young women, meanwhile, are becoming more progressive as gender equality becomes more salient to them. There is truth in parts of this story. Recent elections have shown significant gender differences among young voters, particularly in support for the far right. Young men and women also differ in some gender attitudes, while online ecosystems can amplify highly divergent content. But treating gender conflict as the master explanation risks confusing one of the languages through which discontent is expressed with its deeper sources.

title: Can a fortress be attractive?
content: The final speech before the decisive battle. This is how one might describe the State of the Union address delivered on 16 September by EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to the European Parliament – though with the ambition of speaking to the whole of Europe and the world. It was the last major policy address before the fateful spring of 2027, when elections in France, Italy and Spain (not to mention possible snap elections in Germany) will shape the continent’s political future. An unmissable opportunity to try to spread a message capable of stemming the anti-democratic tide that risks paralysing, if not overwhelming, the entire European project.

title: Sweden’s 2026 election: Social Democrats lost the battle but won the war?
content:
In last week’s parliamentary elections in Sweden, the Swedish Social Democratic Party undoubtedly became the largest party, with the support of 28 per cent of voters and a strong chance of leading the next government by replacing the incumbent right-wing one. Yet, within Swedish Social Democracy, a sense of dissatisfaction prevails. How did this come about?

In a fragmented parliament with eight parties, 28 per cent of the popular vote is not a disaster – especially not from a European perspective. When conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson steps down after four years, it will be the first time since 1994 that a Swedish government has lost power after only a single term.

Yet the 2-point drop to 28 per cent remains historically weak for the Social Democrats. Above all, the contrast with the preceding term is striking. For periods, the party polled between 35 and 37 per cent, and as recently as August, the centre-left opposition bloc held a lead of around ten percentage points. When the results came in, however, the election was decided by a razor-thin margin.

title: A State of the Union bereft of coherence and clarity
content:
The State of the Union is a very special exercise for the president of the European Commission. Its main purpose is to show that the Commission has a clear vision to tackle the numerous challenges and perils the Union is facing, and that, despite the complex environment, there is an experienced pilot at the helm. Indeed, this year’s statement takes place at an exceptionally difficult time, as President Ursula von der Leyen has said from the outset. Her description and diagnosis of the geopolitical and internal challenges and transformation are accurate enough. But what about her answers and political solutions?

Von der Leyen likes to use a certain degree of pathos to appeal to emotions. That is why she invites some special guests to materialise these emotions. One may doubt if pathos is the best way to respond to people’s fears and expectations and to gain trust.

title: Will you stand with civil society?
content: Attacks on civil society are no longer just a problem for those countries and organisations normally associated with democratic backsliding. It is a European trend that, unfortunately, no longer excludes even progressive parties. The arrests of thousands of activists in the UK for holding up signs in support of Palestine Action in the UK under Labour’s rule are a particularly stark example. Progressive parties that are of civil society. Historically sharing roots, constituencies and leaders. Mutually dependent on the creative cross-fertilisation of ideas, experience and trust for our shared success. The current authoritarian winds, therefore, carry a crucial question for progressives: Will you stand with civil society or enable its continuous deterioration?

title: The axis and the alternative
content:
90 years ago, in July 1936, the Bayreuth opera festival featured Richard Wagner’s Siegfried, as it had many times before and since. After this performance, however, one of the festival’s regular guests, who was the leader of Germany at the time, received two envoys from the Spanish nationalist general Francisco Franco. As a result, Germany helped Franco to attack the Spanish Republic from Morocco, and later, Italy also provided massive military support to the fascist forces to wage a civil war on the democratic Republic, which lasted almost three years. 

In 1936, the emerging Italo-German axis sought to suppress, in particular, the possibility that a broad democratic coalition (‘popular front’) would implement social reform in Spain and represent an alternative to their retrograde, violent and chauvinistic politics in the eyes of Europeans. In interwar Europe, democracy was young and fragile. In Italy, it was not given a proper chance. In Germany, in 1933, once the Great Depression destabilised economic and social relations, it was easy to sweep aside the Weimar Republic. The fascists in Germany and Italy even felt they were entitled to impose their views in other countries as well.

title: Good luck! And don’t f**k it up…
content: Remembering the historic turnout of 300,000 Europeans at Budapest Pride 2025, European Social Democrats, led by Rainbow Rose – the lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex and queer organisation associated with the Party of European Socialists (PES) – participated again, on 27 June, in an easy-going and relaxed Pride march. In 2025, Pride was still an illegal event and the heroic mayor of Budapest, Gergely Karácsony, was charged with organising and leading a banned public assembly. This year, the charges were finally dropped during the first week of June, Pride Month. Budapest Pride 2026 then proceeded peacefully, left unhindered by the recently elected prime minister, Péter Magyar.
